title: TOP 15 Most Extreme Corners on Earth Few People Have Ever Seen
fullText: There are 8 billion of us. We have settled every continent on this planet, including Antarctica. There is a town in Siberia where the temperature drops to -67° C and 500 people still wake up, go to work, and send their children to school. There are villages built on the slopes of volcanoes that erupt every single year. There are families living on islands that flood twice a day, every day, and they simply build higher. Humans live everywhere. Except here. There was a place where the ground itself reaches 80° C. There is an island where your government made it a crime to set foot on the sand. There is a valley where it has not rained in 2 million years. And there is a spot on this planet so far from everything that when the International Space Station passes overhead, the astronauts inside are the closest human beings to it. These are the 15 most extreme corners of Earth where no one has ever lived. Stay until the end because number one is a place where researchers say the air will injure your lungs the moment you inhale it. Not after an hour on the first breath. And before we start, tell me in the comments where you are watching from right now. Last time we had people from over 40 countries watching at the same time. Let us see if you can beat that. Tonight we begin in the middle of the largest hot desert on Earth at a place the people living on its edges named the land of terror. Number 15, the Tenez roofed basin, Algeria and Mali. The Sahara covers 9 million square kilm and people live across almost all of it. Nomads, traders, oasis towns, entire cities. But there is a region in the south central Sahara, roughly the size of Germany, where none of that exists. No oasis, no well, no vegetation of any kind. For more than 700 kilometers in any direction, there is nothing but flat gravel and sand. The Tuareg called it Tanzroof, which translates roughly to the land of thirst or the land of terror, depending on the dialect. They did not name it that for poetry. They named it that because caravans that entered it did not always come out. Here is what makes it different from every other stretch of desert you have seen. The Tenez roof has almost no dunes. It is flat, featureless, and that is exactly the problem. With no landmarks, no rock formations, and no vegetation, travelers historically had nothing to navigate by. There is a documented history of vehicles running out of fuel while driving in circles inside it. Daytime surface temperatures pass 50° C. Annual rainfall in the driest sections is close to zero. There is a single paved road crossing part of it built in the 20th century and drivers are advised never to travel it alone. Nobody has ever built a permanent settlement here, not once in the entire history of the Sahara. An empty desert at least lets you walk away. The next place looks like an ordinary green island off the coast of Scotland. And for 48 years, walking onto it could have killed you. Number 14, Grunard Islands, Scotland. It is small, 2 km long, 1 km wide, covered in grass and heather, sitting quietly in a bay off the northwest coast of Scotland. From the mainland, it looks like every other Hebradian island, green, windswept, harmless. In 1942, the British government bought it and released anthrax spores on it. The tests were part of a biological weapons program during the Second World War. Sheep were tethered across the island. Bombs containing basillus anthrais were detonated. The sheep died within days and then the scientists discovered something they had not planned for. The spores did not break down. They sank into the soil and they stayed viable. Grunard was quarantined. Signs were posted. Landing was prohibited by law and it stayed that way for 48 years because anthrax spores can survive in soil for decades and nobody had a way to remove them. The cleanup finally happened between 1986 and 1990. 280 tons of formaldahhide diluted in seawater were sprayed across the entire island and the most contaminated top soil was dug out and taken away. In 1990, the quarantine was lifted and the warning signs came down. The island is now legally safe to visit and still nobody lives there. A handful of sheep graze on it. Researchers have gone back to sample the soil, but no person has made a home on Grunard since the tests, and the families who owned it before the war never returned. Some things you can decontaminate. Reputation is harder. Poison keeps you off that island. The next place keeps you off with nothing but geometry. It is a wall of rock coming straight out of the ocean, and it [clears throat] is the tallest thing of its kind on the planet. Number 13, Balls Pyramid, Australia. 600 km off the east coast of Australia, a blade of black volcanic rock comes out of the Pacific and climbs 562 m into the sky. That is taller than the Empire State Building. [music] At its base, it is barely a kilometer long. It is the eroded core of a shield volcano that collapsed around 7 million years ago. Everything soft washed away. What is left is the hard center standing alone in open ocean with waves hitting it from every direction. There is no beach, no flat ground anywhere, no fresh water. Climbing it was banned outright in 1982. So naturally, in 2001, a team of Australian scientists climbed it at night. They were looking for a bug, specifically the Lord How Island stick insect, a creature about the size of your hand that had been declared extinct in 1920 after rats got loose on the island next door. Locals used to call them tree lobsters, which is both an accurate description and I think a slightly unfair one. 100 m up a near vertical face under a single scraggly shrub growing out of a crack in the rock, they found 24 of them alive. 24 insects, one bush, a sea stack in the middle of the Pacific. That was the entire population of the species, and it had been sitting there for 80 years while the rest of the world assumed they were gone. No human has ever lived on Ball's pyramid, and no human ever will. But something did. It just needed a very small bush and absolutely no neighbors. Number 12, the Valley of Death, Kamchatka, Russia. Discovered in 1975, 2 km long. And the first thing the researchers saw when they walked in was the bodies. Foxes, bears, wolverines, ravens, dozens of animals lying on the valley floor, most of them intact, some of them fresh. The valley sits over volcanic vents leaking carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulfide. Both gases are heavier than air, so on a still day, they settle into the low ground in an invisible layer. A small animal walks through it and goes down within minutes. A scavenger arrives to feed on the body and goes down beside it. Researchers have watched that chain repeat three and four times over a single carcass. When the wind blows, it is harmless. When the wind stops, there is no smell, no color, and no sound to warn you. Scientists go in for a few minutes at a time. Nobody goes in twice on the same day. Number 11, Ila Dada Grande, Brazil. 33 kilometers off the coast of Sao Paulo, there is an island of 43 hectares covered in forest that the Brazilian government has made it illegal for you to visit. 11,000 years ago, rising sea levels cut this piece of land off from the mainland. The golden lance head vipers stranded on it found themselves with no predators and also with no prey because everything they normally ate was on the other side of the water. So they looked up. The only food left was migratory birds resting in the canopy. But birds do not politely lie down and wait to die. A snake that bites one and loses it in flight has wasted a meal. So the venom got faster. Estimates put the golden lance head at roughly three to five times more potent than its mainland cousins, strong enough to start destroying tissue almost on contact. Population estimates run from 2,000 to 4,000 snakes on that island. In the densest sections, that works out to about one snake per square meter, which is roughly one snake for every place you might consider putting a foot. Landing is banned without a federal permit, and permits go almost exclusively to researchers. The permit comes with a condition. You have to bring a doctor with you. Not a guide, a doctor. There was a lighthouse there once with a keeper and his family living beside it. It was automated in the 1920s. The story the fishermen on the mainland still tell is that the snakes came in through the windows one night. Nobody has lived on Katada Grande since. Venom keeps you out of that forest. The next place has no forest, no shade, and pools of liquid that will take the soles off your boots. Number 10, Dal, Ethiopia. In the Danakill depression, more than 100 m below sea level, sits what may be the strangest ground on this planet. Neon yellow crusts, green pools that bubble, orange spires of salt, ponds of liquid so acidic that measured values approach a pH of zero. Between 1960 and 1966, weather records at Dal registered an average annual temperature of about 34.6° C, the highest average of any inhabited weather station ever recorded. Daytime highs regularly pass 45° C. There is no shade of any kind anywhere for kilometers. In 2019, a study published in Nature Ecology and Evolution by a team including researchers from the French National Center for Scientific Research examined the hyper acidic hypers saline pools at Dal and reached a conclusion nobody expected. Some of those pools contain no life whatsoever. Not extreaphile bacteria, not archa, nothing. The Afar people live in the wider Danakill region and have mined salt there for centuries. Camel caravans still cross it, but nobody lives at Dal itself. The mining outpost that operated there in the early 20th century was abandoned decades ago, and what is left of the buildings is slowly dissolving into the ground. We keep finding life inside nuclear reactors and inside boiling deep sea vents. And then there is a warm green pool in Ethiopia with absolutely nothing in it. Dal is small enough to walk across in an afternoon. The next one is 650,000 km and it swallowed a city whole. Number nine, the empty quarter, Arabian Peninsula. In 1946, a British explorer named Wilfried Thesser set out to cross the largest continuous sand desert on Earth with a small group of Bedu companions and a string of camels. He had been warned. The Rub Alcali, the empty quarter, spreads across parts of Saudi Arabia, Oman, Yemen, and the United Arab Emirates. The dunes reach 250 m. Summer temperatures pass 50° C. In the interior, some years produced no rain at all. Fesser later wrote that the crossing was only possible because the men with him carried in their heads the location of wells that were sometimes weeks apart and that a single navigational error meant death for the entire party. Not hardship, death. He did it twice. And under all that sand, there is something. In 1992, a team studying satellite images noticed faint lines converging on a single point at the desert's edge in Oman. ancient caravan tracks pressed into the ground by centuries of camels, all pointing at the same place. They dug there and found a fortress with eight towers that had collapsed into a limestone sinkhole underneath it. Some of them believe they had found Ubar, the city described in Arab tradition, as having been swallowed by the sand as punishment for its arrogance. Whether or not that identification holds, the fortress is real, and the story it tells is the same either way. People came to the edge of the empty quarter. They built something. They traded frankincense out of it for centuries. And then the desert took it back and hid it so completely that it took a satellite to find the road. The interior itself has never held a settlement. Not in recorded history and not before it. The empty quarter is empty because of heat. The next place is empty because of cold and it is the largest uninhabited island on this planet. Number eight, Devon Island, Canada. 55,000 square km of rock and gravel in the Canadian Arctic. That is bigger than Croatia and there is not a single permanent resident anywhere on it. The reason is straightforward. It sits above the Arctic Circle. Summer averages hover just above freezing. Winter drops below -50° C. The ground is a polar desert of frost shattered stone with almost nothing growing on it. Near the center of the island, there is a crater 23 km wide punched into the ground by an impact roughly 39 million years ago. It is called H Hotton Crater and the combination of that crater, the perafrost, the barren rock in the complete isolation makes Devon Island the closest thing to Mars available on this planet. Since 1997, NASA and the Mars Institute have run the hoten Mars project there. Researchers live in habitat modules for weeks at a time. Drive pressurized rovers across the rubble and practice working in space suits. When you see photographs of astronaut training on a red, brown rocky plane that looks like nowhere on Earth, there is a decent chance you are looking at Devon Island. People have tried to live there. Inuit hunters used it seasonally for generations. There was a Royal Canadianmounted police post at Dundas Harbor in the 1920s. In 1934, families were relocated there from Baffan Island. They lasted 2 years. Since then, the largest uninhabited island on Earth has stayed exactly that. Number seven, Bouvet Island. In 1964, a South African expedition landed on a glacier island in the South Atlantic and found a lifeboat sitting in a lagoon. It was abandoned. There were ores nearby. There were supplies. There was no crew, no bodies, no note, and no wreckage anywhere on the shore. No ship had been reported missing in that part of the ocean. The boat carried no markings that anyone could trace. To understand how strange that is, you need to know where they were standing. Bouvet Island is the most remote island on Earth. It sits in the South Atlantic, roughly 1,600 km north of Antarctica. The nearest land of any kind is uninhabited. The nearest land with people on it is Tristan Duna, 2,200 km away. The island itself is 50 km of volcanic rock and about 93% of it is buried under a glacier. The coastline is almost entirely ice cliff dropping straight into freezing water, which is why most modern landings are made by helicopter rather than by boat. It was first cited in 1739 by a French explorer who wrote down the wrong coordinates. Then it vanished. James Cook went looking for it and could not find it. It was not reliably located again until 1808, 69 years later. Norway claimed it in 1927. Today, there is an automated weather station and an unmanned research hut, which has already been rebuilt once after the weather flattened it. That is the entire human presence on the island. Which brings us back to the lifeboat. Someone reached the most isolated island on this planet in an open boat and climbed out of it. And then as far as anyone has ever been able to establish, nothing. Bouvet is defined by distance. The next place is defined by heat that no living tissue can survive. Number six, the loot desert, Iran. In 2021, an analysis published in the Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society changed what we thought we knew about heat on this planet. Researchers examined land surface temperature readings collected by NASA's modus instruments between 2002 and 2019 covering the entire globe and found the single highest reading anywhere on Earth 80.8° C in the dashed elute in southeastern Iran. To be precise about what that means, air temperature is measured about 1 1/2 m above the ground in the shade. That is the number on your weather app. Land surface temperature is the heat of the ground itself. The loot holds the record for the hottest ground ever measured on this planet. The desert covers about 51,000 square km and is surrounded by mountains that trap hot air and stop it from escaping. Parts of it are covered in yardangs, enormous ridges carved by wind, some of them 75 m tall and running in parallel lines for kilometers. UNESCO, which listed the loot as a world heritage site in 2016, notes that these formations are clearly visible from space. If you stood in the middle of the loot in July, the air around your face would be roughly 50°. The ground under your boots would be 80. That is a 30° difference between your head and your feet, and it is the reason nothing grows there, nothing crawls there, and nobody stays. There are settlements at the edges. There is nothing in the middle. There never has been. If you have made it this far, you are exactly the kind of person this channel was built for. Subscribe so the next one finds you. Number five, Runit Dome, Marshall Islands. On Runit Island, part of Enowitak atal in the Pacific, there is a concrete dome 45 cm thick and about 110 m across. The people of the Marshall Islands call it the tomb. Between 1948 and 1958, the United States conducted 43 nuclear tests at Anowita. When the testing ended, thousands of cubic meters of radioactive soil and debris were spread across the atal. [music] In the late 1970s, around 4,000 American servicemen were sent in to clean it up. They scraped the contaminated top soil, mixed it with concrete, and poured it into an existing crater that had been left by one of the detonations. Then they capped the whole thing. The dome was finished in 1980. It holds roughly 85,000 cub m of radioactive material including plutonium 239 which has a half-life of just over 24,000 years. And it has a design problem that was understood from the very beginning. The bottom of the crater was never lined. There is no barrier at all between the radioactive material and the porous coral underneath it. Seawater moves through that coral freely. A 2013 Department of Energy report acknowledged that the sediment in the surrounding lagoon is already contaminated and suggested that the contents of the dome and the lagoon may already be in a kind of equilibrium. Rising sea levels add a second problem and studies have raised the concern that rising water could eventually compromise the structure itself. The people of Anowto were removed from their home islands for the testing. Parts of the atal were later resettled. Runit Island was not. Nobody lives on it and nobody is expected to for a very long time. Every other place on this list has been uninhabitable since before we existed. This one we made. Radiation is what keeps us off ruin it. The next place we could walk onto tomorrow with no protection at all and we still could not live there because it has not rained there in recorded history. Number four, Yungai, Adakama Desert, Chile. The Adakama is the driest non-polar desert on Earth. There are weather stations inside it that have never recorded a single drop of rain in their entire operating history. Some riverbeds show evidence of having been dry for over 120,000 years. But there is one specific area near a place called Yungai that is the driest of all of it. In 2003, a team led by the Mexican researcher Raphael Navaro Gonzalez working with NASA ran an experiment there. They collected soil from the Yungai region and applied the same test that the Viking landers had used to search for life on Mars back in 1976. The results came back looking exactly like the Viking results had. No cultivable bacteria. In the most extreme samples, essentially no detectable organic material at all. The soil was for all practical purposes sterile. The findings were published in the journal Science and they changed how astrobiologists read the original Mars data. Three things combined to make it that dry. The Andes block moisture coming from the Amazon. The Chilean coastal range blocks moisture coming off the Pacific and a cold ocean current running along the coast suppresses evaporation before it can even start. Between the three of them, water simply never arrives. There are towns in the Adakama. There are mines, observatories, and highways. But at the core, in the driest sections around Yungai, there is no settlement, no agriculture, and no water. That ground has been dead longer than our species has been alive. In Chile, dryness is measured in decades without rain. In the next place, it is measured in millions of years. Number three, the McMmero Dry Valleys, Antarctica. Antarctica is covered in ice with one enormous exception. In Victoria land near McMmero Sound, there is a region of roughly 4,800 km where there is no ice at all. Bare rock, bare gravel, frozen soil. The cause is the catabatic wind. Cold, dense air pours down off the polar plateau and accelerates as it falls, sometimes reaching 320 kmh. That air is so dry and moving so fast that it turns ice and snow directly into vapor without melting them first. Nothing accumulates. Nothing collects. It simply leaves. Parts of the dry valleys are estimated to have been free of ice and free of rain for as long as 2 million years. There are mummified seals on the valley floors, kilometers inland from the sea, some carbonated at over a thousand years old. Nobody is entirely certain why they walk that far in the wrong direction. They are not decomposing because there is nothing there capable of decomposing them. They are simply drying out very slowly in the same position they stopped in. There is life. There are microbes in the soil and there are lakes sealed under permanent ice caps. One of them so salty that it stays liquid far below freezing. But there is nothing you can see. No plants, no animals, no movement except the wind. The valleys are one of the most strictly protected environments on the planet. Access is limited and everything carried in has to be carried back out, including human waste, because nothing there is capable of breaking it down. Everything so far has been ground you could physically stand on. The next entry is a coordinate in open water where the closest people to you are not on the surface of this planet at all. Number two, Point Nemo. In 1992, a Croatian Canadian survey engineer named Hervoy Lucatella set a computer to solve a geometry problem. He wanted the single point in the world's oceans that sits at the maximum possible distance from any land. The answer came back at 48° 52.6 minutes south, 123° 23.6 minutes west. Deep in the South Pacific, roughly halfway between New Zealand and Chile. The nearest land is 2,688 km away. That is not the distance in one direction. That is the distance in every direction. Three small scraps of land sit at almost exactly that range. Ducy Island to the north, Motui near Easter Island to the northeast, and Mar Island off the Antarctic coast to the south. All three of them are uninhabited, which means there is no human being inside an area of roughly 22 million km surrounding that point. That is an area larger than Russia. The International Space Station orbits at about 400 km up. So when the station passes overhead, the astronauts inside it are more than six times closer to Point Nemo than any person standing on land anywhere on Earth. The closest humans to the most isolated coordinate on this planet are usually not on the planet. Lucatella never went there. By his own account, it is entirely possible that no human being has ever passed through those exact coordinates. There is barely anything alive in the water either. Point Nemo sits inside the South Pacific Gy, a slow rotating current system that keeps nutrients out of the region. In 2019, researchers from the Maxplank Institute for Marine Microbiology sampled the area and reported some of the lowest cell counts ever measured in ocean surface water anywhere. And because it is the emptiest place on the planet, we use it as a graveyard. Decommissioned satellites, cargo vessels, and the mere space station were all deliberately brought down into this stretch of ocean. There is more human hardware sitting on that seafloor than in most working harbors. Point Nemo is defined by distance. Number one is defined by something much simpler. It is the coldest place that exists on the surface of this planet. And the people who study it say the human body cannot process the air there. Number one, the East Antarctic Plateau. Between two high points on the Antarctic ice sheet called Dome Argus and Dome Fuji, more than 3,500 m above sea level, there is a stretch of ridge where the coldest temperatures ever recorded on this planet occur. In 2013, a team led by Ted Scambos at the National Snow and Ice Data Center at the University of Colorado Boulder analyzed 32 years of satellite data and found surface temperatures reaching - 93° C. That already broke the previous record set at Russia's Vastto station in 1983. Then in 2018 they revised it publishing in geoysical research letters using recalibrated satellite readings collected between 2004 in 2016. The team reported nearly 100 separate locations reaching - 98° C - 98. Scambo stated that this appears to be roughly as cold as it is physically possible for the surface of the earth to get. And here is what he said about being there. He said he had never been in conditions that cold and that he hoped he never would be. He said that every breath is painful and that you have to be extremely careful not to freeze part of your throat or your lungs while inhaling. That is not a figure of speech. At those temperatures, the act of breathing damages tissue. The conditions required are very specific. The sky has to stay clear for several days. The air has to be extraordinarily dry because any water vapor at all would trap heat near the surface. When both of those hold, the snow radiates its remaining warmth straight out into space and cold air sinks into shallow hollows in the ice, sometimes only a couple of meters deep, where it settles and drops further. There is no station there. Vastto, the coldest permanently staffed base on Earth, sits at a lower elevation and is not even inside the coldest zone. Those pockets have never been measured from the ground by anyone. It is the only place on this list that no human has ever stood in at the moment it reached its extreme. We found the coldest place on Earth and we found it from orbit because going there was never seriously on the table. 15 corners of a planet that 8 billion of us have otherwise covered completely. A basin in the Sahara with no landmarks to steer by. An island quarantined for 48 years over what was buried in its soil. A rock in the Pacific where 24 insects outlasted their own extinction. A valley in Russia where the air pools and stops. An island where the snakes moved into the trees. Pools in Ethiopia with nothing living in them. A desert that swallowed a city and hid the road. The largest uninhabited island in the world. The most remote island in the world. And an abandoned lifeboat nobody can explain. The hottest ground ever measured. A concrete tomb over a nuclear crater. Soil in Chile that came back sterile. Valleys with no rain in 2 million years. A coordinate where the nearest people are in orbit. And a ridge of ice where breathing hurts. Here is what strikes me about this list. Two of these places are so far outside normal conditions that space agencies rehearse other planets in them. And the coldest one we have never actually stood in at all. We measured it from space because going there was never seriously on the table. We are a remarkably stubborn animal. We built cities in deserts, on perafrost, on the flanks of active volcanoes, and in the middle of open ocean. But there is a line. And these 15 places are what sits on the other side of it. Which one surprised you the most? Tell me in the comments. And if you made it all the way here, you already know this channel was built for people exactly like you. Hit subscribe. Turn on notifications. The next video takes you somewhere even more impossible. We will see you there.
fullTextVi: Có 8 tỷ người trong chúng ta. Chúng ta đã định cư ở mọi lục địa trên hành tinh này, bao gồm cả Nam Cực. Có một thị trấn ở Siberia có nhiệt độ giảm xuống -67° C và 500 người vẫn thức dậy, đi làm và đưa con đi học. Có những ngôi làng được xây dựng trên sườn núi lửa phun trào hàng năm. Có những gia đình sống trên những hòn đảo ngập nước hai lần một ngày, và họ chỉ đơn giản là xây dựng cao hơn. Con người sống ở khắp mọi nơi. Ngoại trừ ở đây. Có nơi mặt đất đã lên tới 80° C. Có một hòn đảo nơi chính phủ của bạn quy định việc đặt chân đến là tội ác trên cát. Có một thung lũng đã không mưa suốt 2 triệu năm. Và có một nơi trên hành tinh này cách xa mọi thứ mà khi Trạm vũ trụ quốc tế bay qua trên cao, các phi hành gia bên trong là những con người gần gũi nhất đến nó. Đây là 15 góc cực đoan nhất của Trái đất mà chưa ai từng đến đã sống. Hãy ở lại đến cuối cùng vì số một là nơi mà các nhà nghiên cứu cho rằng không khí sẽ làm tổn thương phổi của bạn ngay khi bạn hít vào. Không sau một giờ ở hơi thở đầu tiên. Và trước khi chúng ta bắt đầu, hãy cho tôi biết trong phần nhận xét nơi bạn đang xem ngay lập tức. Lần trước chúng tôi đã có người từ hơn 40 quốc gia xem cùng một lúc. Hãy để chúng tôi xem liệu bạn có thể đánh bại điều đó không. Tối nay chúng ta bắt đầu ở giữa sa mạc nóng bỏng lớn nhất trên Trái đất tại một nơi mà người dân sống ở rìa của nó được mệnh danh là vùng đất khủng bố. Số 15, lưu vực mái nhà Tenez, Algeria và Mali. Sahara có diện tích 9 triệu kilômét vuông và con người sống ở hầu hết it. Những người du mục, thương nhân, thị trấn ốc đảo, toàn bộ thành phố. Nhưng có một khu vực ở trung tâm phía nam Sahara, có diện tích gần bằng Đức, nơi không có thứ đó tồn tại. Không có ốc đảo, không có giếng nước, không có thảm thực vật nào cả. Hơn 700 km về mọi hướng chẳng có gì ngoài sỏi phẳng và cát. Người Tuareg gọi nó là Tanzroof, dịch nôm na là vùng đất khát khao hay vùng đất khủng bố, tùy theo phương ngữ. Họ không đặt tên đó cho thơ. Họ đặt tên như vậy vì những đoàn lữ hành đi vào không phải lúc nào cũng đi ra. Đây là điều làm cho nó khác biệt với mọi vùng sa mạc khác mà bạn có seen. Mái nhà Tenez hầu như không có cồn cát. Nó bằng phẳng, không có gì đặc biệt và đó chính xác là vấn đề. Không có địa danh, không có khối đá và không có thảm thực vật, trong lịch sử du khách không có gì để điều hướng bằng. segments.viText: Chúng tôi đã xây dựng các thành phố trên sa mạc, trên vùng băng vĩnh cửu, bên sườn những ngọn núi lửa đang hoạt động và

segments.text: in the middle of open ocean.
segments.viText: giữa đại dương rộng mở.

segments.text: But there is a line.
segments.viText: Nhưng có một dòng.

segments.text: And these 15 places are what sits on the other side of it.
segments.viText: Và 15 địa điểm này nằm ở phía bên kia của nó.

segments.text: Which one surprised you the most?
segments.viText: Điều nào làm bạn ngạc nhiên nhất?

segments.text: Tell me in the comments.
segments.viText: Hãy cho tôi biết trong phần bình luận.

segments.text: And if you made it all the way here, you already know this channel
segments.viText: Và nếu bạn đã làm được đến đây thì bạn đã biết đến kênh này

segments.text: was built for people exactly like you.
segments.viText: được xây dựng cho những người giống hệt như bạn.

segments.text: Hit subscribe.
segments.viText: Nhấn đăng ký.

segments.text: Turn on notifications.
segments.viText: Bật thông báo.

segments.text: The next video takes you somewhere even more impossible.
segments.viText: Video tiếp theo sẽ đưa bạn đến một nơi thậm chí còn khó tin hơn.

segments.text: We will see you there.
segments.viText: Chúng tôi sẽ gặp bạn ở đó.
